findings.explanation: `writeText` is blocking and non-cancellable, so a cancelled save may continue writing concurrently with its replacement and leave an older or corrupted draft on disk.

findings.title: A failed like can roll back a newer toggle
findings.explanation: Each request captures its own previous post and rolls back unconditionally, so an earlier request that fails can overwrite the optimistic state of a later toggle.

findings.title: Overlapping refreshes report loading incorrectly
findings.explanation: Each refresh independently sets `isLoading` false on completion, so the first of multiple overlapping refreshes can hide the loading indicator while another refresh is still running.

findings.title: Unexpected draft JSON shapes can escape restoration
findings.explanation: The parser only catches I/O and serialization exceptions, while accessing `jsonObject` on a valid non-object JSON value can throw an unchecked exception and fail the launched coroutine.

findings.title: Concurrent cache misses are not coalesced
findings.explanation: Two callers missing the same key can both fetch from the backend before either populates the cache, causing avoidable duplicate requests and potentially overwhelming a slow or rate-limited backend.

findings.title: A slower fetch can overwrite a newer cached profile
findings.explanation: Concurrent misses for the same ID insert results in completion order, so an older, slower backend response can replace a newer result that was already cached.

findings.title: LIKE wildcards in the prefix are treated as patterns
findings.explanation: Appending `%` does not implement a literal name prefix when `name_prefix` contains `%` or `_`; those characters broaden the search unless they are escaped and the query declares the escape character.

findings.title: Expiry arithmetic can overflow
findings.explanation: The unchecked cast and subtraction can wrap or panic for extreme timestamps (including `i64::MIN`), so compute the difference with checked or saturating arithmetic.

findings.title: Shutdown leaves connection tasks running
findings.explanation: `run_until` returns without tracking or aborting the spawned handlers, so connected clients remain serviced and keep the log file open after the server is supposedly stopped.

findings.title: `read_line` is not cancellation-safe in this select
findings.explanation: When a broadcast or idle timer wins, the pending `read_line` future is dropped and may lose already-read partial input, corrupting or discarding a client's next line.

findings.title: Unbounded line reads allow memory exhaustion
findings.explanation: A client can send an arbitrarily long nickname or message without a newline, causing `read_line` to grow its buffer without limit.

findings.title: Clients can receive broadcasts from before they joined
findings.explanation: The receiver is subscribed before nickname validation and user-count registration, so messages sent while the client is logging in remain queued and may be delivered after it joins.

findings.title: Accept errors are silently retried
findings.explanation: Continuing on every accept error can create a tight retry loop during persistent failures, consuming CPU while hiding the underlying server error.

findings.title: Configured listen address is not used
findings.explanation: `main` prints `config.listen_addr` but binds the chat server to `CHAT_LISTEN` or a hard-coded default, so the configured address is ignored and the startup message can be misleading.

findings.title: Lagged receivers silently lose messages
findings.explanation: When a client falls behind the bounded broadcast channel, messages are dropped without any notification, making message loss invisible to the client.

findings.title: Message formatting strips trailing whitespace
findings.explanation: `trim_end()` removes all trailing whitespace from message text rather than only the line terminator, unexpectedly changing messages.

findings.title: Changes are discarded while advancing the cursor
findings.explanation: Each page’s `items` are never consumed, yet its cursor is persisted, so changes are permanently skipped instead of being applied.

findings.title: Cancellation is recorded as a sync failure
findings.explanation: Catching `Throwable` includes `CancellationException`, so normal coroutine cancellation updates the error status and can misreport an interrupted sync as a failure.

findings.title: Some sync failures bypass status reporting
findings.explanation: `accounts()` and `loadCursors()` run before the `try`, so failures there propagate without calling `statusStore.reportError`.

findings.title: Repeated cursors can make paging loop forever
findings.explanation: If the API returns the same non-null `nextCursor` repeatedly, the loop keeps requesting the same page with no progress or termination check.

findings.title: A failed run permanently stops periodic syncing
findings.explanation: An exception from `sync().collect()` escapes the launched coroutine and terminates the periodic loop, so later scheduled attempts never run.

findings.title: Cursor writes can leave the store corrupted
findings.explanation: Writing directly to the destination file is not atomic, so a crash or overlapping sync can leave truncated JSON that `loadCursors()` silently treats as an empty cursor map.

findings.title: Concurrent sync runs can race on cursor state
findings.explanation: Multiple collectors or periodic/manual runs can load and write the same cursor file concurrently, allowing one run to overwrite another run’s newer cursors.

findings.title: Shutdown leaves client tasks running
findings.explanation: Returning from `run` drops the listener but does not signal or await the detached client tasks, so existing connections remain open and continue using shared state after the server has ostensibly shut down.

findings.title: Broadcast traffic can indefinitely reset the idle timeout
findings.explanation: The timeout is recreated each time this `select!` loop iterates, so a client receiving frequent broadcasts can avoid the idle timeout even if it sends no data.

findings.title: Lagged clients silently miss messages
findings.explanation: When a client falls behind the bounded broadcast channel, `Lagged` is ignored and the skipped messages are permanently lost without notifying the client or otherwise handling the gap.

findings.title: Logging failures are silently discarded
findings.explanation: All file write and flush errors are ignored, so the server can continue claiming to log every message while silently losing log entries, including after disk or filesystem failures.

findings.title: Unbounded input lines allow memory exhaustion
findings.explanation: `Lines::next_line()` buffers until a newline with no length limit, allowing a client to send an arbitrarily large line and consume unbounded server memory.

findings.title: Message text loses trailing whitespace
findings.explanation: `trim_end()` removes all trailing whitespace from chat content rather than only the line terminator, changing messages that intentionally end in spaces or tabs.

findings.title: Concurrent cache misses duplicate backend requests
findings.explanation: The cache lock is released before fetching, so simultaneous loads for the same uncached ID all call the backend and race to insert, defeating the cache's request-coalescing purpose under concurrency.

findings.title: Cache grows without bound
findings.explanation: Entries are only checked for expiration on lookup and never removed, so a long-running service seeing many distinct IDs retains expired profiles indefinitely.

findings.title: Backend async method does not require Send futures
findings.explanation: Because the trait's async method has no `Send` bound, `ProfileService::load` may produce a non-`Send` future and therefore cannot be used with common Tokio APIs such as `tokio::spawn` for some backend implementations.

findings.title: LIKE wildcards are not escaped
findings.explanation: Parameter binding prevents SQL injection, but `%` and `_` in `name_prefix` retain wildcard meaning, so inputs are not treated as literal prefixes and can match unintended names.

findings.title: Expiry arithmetic can wrap for large timestamps
findings.explanation: Casting the public `u64` expiry timestamp to `i64` can wrap values above `i64::MAX`, producing an incorrect remaining lifetime or overflowing the subtraction.

findings.title: System clock adjustment can panic expiry checks
findings.explanation: A system clock before the Unix epoch triggers `expect` and panics, despite this being a recoverable clock condition for a helper that otherwise returns a duration.

findings.title: `INFO_FILE` may not be a supported genrule variable
findings.explanation: If Bazel does not recognize `$(INFO_FILE)` as a genrule Make variable, analysis fails with an undefined-variable error, so the generated `version.py` target cannot build; use a supported status-file mechanism, such as a stamping rule that declares the status file as an input.

findings.title: Integration test does not detect extra local rates
findings.explanation: The loop only checks states returned by the service, so stale entries present only in `RATES` pass unnoticed; compare the complete state sets before checking rate values.

findings.title: Manifest paths are not repo-relative
findings.explanation: `File.path` is an execroot-relative artifact path and can include configuration-specific `bazel-out` prefixes or external-repository paths, so the manifest does not reliably contain the repo-relative paths promised by the rule's documentation.

findings.title: Genrule arguments are not shell-quoted
findings.explanation: The expanded tool and source paths are inserted unquoted into a shell command, so valid workspace or artifact paths containing spaces or shell metacharacters can cause the command to fail or interpret unintended arguments.

findings.title: `ctx.actions.write` cannot accept an Args object
findings.explanation: `ctx.actions.write` requires `content` to be a string, so passing `args` causes analysis to fail for every `py_bundle` target.

findings.title: Flaky setting can conceal the timing failure
findings.explanation: Marking the test flaky allows Bazel to retry and accept intermittent failures, leaving the known timing bug unresolved and potentially hiding regressions.

findings.title: Resolving `__file__` can escape the Bazel runfiles tree
findings.explanation: `Path.resolve()` follows Bazel’s runfiles symlink for `tax.py` back to the source tree, so the adjacent CSV lookup can fail when the deployed runtime has runfiles but not the original checkout.

findings.title: The live-service URL is a reserved example domain
findings.explanation: `rates.example.com` is a placeholder domain rather than a usable rates service, so this integration test cannot reliably reach the service it claims to validate.

findings.title: The documented command filters out the test
findings.explanation: `--test_tag_filters=-manual` excludes this test because it is tagged `manual`, so the stated command will not execute it.

findings.title: The comparison does not detect missing live states
findings.explanation: The loop only checks states returned by the service, so the test passes if the service omits states that are present in the bundled rates.

findings.title: SSRF check can be bypassed by DNS resolution
findings.explanation: The check only examines the URL hostname, so a public-looking hostname that resolves (or is rebound) to a private or metadata IP can make `fetch` access internal services; validate resolved addresses and constrain the actual connection, including redirects.

findings.title: Remote imports have no timeout or response-size limit
findings.explanation: An authenticated caller can make the service wait indefinitely or buffer an arbitrarily large response with `res.text()`, consuming connections and memory; apply a timeout and enforce a maximum response size.

findings.title: Malformed note IDs become internal errors
findings.explanation: `decodeURIComponent` throws for malformed percent escapes, causing the outer handler to return a 500 instead of treating the path as an invalid ID and returning a client error or 404.

findings.title: Internal exception details are returned to clients
findings.explanation: Returning arbitrary exception messages in the 500 response can expose database, infrastructure, or other sensitive implementation details; log the error server-side and return a generic response.

findings.title: Signup uniqueness check is vulnerable to races
findings.explanation: Two concurrent signups can both pass `findByEmail` and attempt creation, so the database must enforce email uniqueness and the conflict must be handled as a 409 rather than surfacing as a 500.

findings.title: Import failures expose upstream error details
findings.explanation: The response includes raw fetch exception messages, which may disclose internal network or URL details; return a generic import error and keep diagnostics in server-side logs.

findings.title: Malformed cookie encoding can turn requests into 500s
findings.explanation: `decodeURIComponent` throws for malformed percent escapes, and this exception propagates through authentication into the router’s generic 500 response instead of treating the cookie as invalid.

findings.title: IPv6 private-address checks can be bypassed
findings.explanation: The prefix checks miss equivalent IPv6 spellings and other non-public ranges such as IPv4-mapped addresses written in hexadecimal or expanded form, allowing imports to reach private or loopback destinations.

findings.title: DNS resolution leaves import vulnerable to SSRF
findings.explanation: The URL is checked by hostname string only, so a public-looking hostname resolving to a private address can access internal services, and the comment’s suggested network-layer mitigation is not enforced here.

findings.title: Import timeout does not cover response-body reads
findings.explanation: The abort timeout is attached to `fetch`, but the fetch promise resolves once headers arrive, so a server can stall the body indefinitely and hold the request open while `readLimited` waits.

findings.title: Body reader is cancelled even after normal completion
findings.explanation: The `finally` block calls `reader.cancel()` even when the stream is already complete, which can reject or interfere with stream implementations and can mask an earlier read/size error if cancellation itself throws.

findings.title: Signup has a username-creation race
findings.explanation: The separate lookup and create are not atomic, so concurrent signups for the same username can both pass the check unless the database enforces a unique constraint and the conflict is handled.

findings.title: PATCH can update a note after ownership changes
findings.explanation: Ownership is checked with an initial read and the subsequent update is keyed only by note ID, allowing a concurrent ownership change or deletion/recreation to cause an unauthorized update unless the database operation also enforces the user ID.

findings.title: Search assumes a specific SQL dialect and row shape
findings.explanation: The `?` placeholders and `ESCAPE` literal are dialect-specific, while `Db.query` promises only `unknown[]`, so the endpoint may fail or return an invalid/untyped response for otherwise conforming database adapters.

findings.title: Non-success imports leave the response body unconsumed
findings.explanation: Returning immediately for a non-OK response does not cancel or drain its body, which can waste network resources or prevent connection reuse in runtimes that require explicit body cleanup.

findings.title: Invalid or misleading Content-Length is not handled safely
findings.explanation: The size check trusts a parseable declared length only when it exceeds the cap; malformed, negative, or inaccurate values bypass it, and the subsequent stream limit remains the only reliable enforcement.

findings.title: Malformed percent-encoding in note IDs becomes a 500
findings.explanation: `decodeURIComponent` can throw for an invalid escape sequence and is evaluated inside the route-level catch, so a malformed path returns an internal-server-error response rather than a client error.

findings.title: Caller headers can override the JSON content type
findings.explanation: Spreading caller-supplied headers after the default permits an inconsistent content type for JSON responses, making the helper’s response contract easy to violate.
